proof_skeleton_nl: Define the admissible set S of exponents. First prove a lower bound by explicit construction: L1 shows that g(n)=n^2 works for every r\le 1/4, so in particular 1/4\in S. For the upper bound, fix any r>1/4 and assume there is a witness g. By L2, g is strictly increasing and hence g(n)\ge n. Because r>0, L3 shows that the difference sequence d_n=g(n+1)-g(n) is nondecreasing. With monotone differences, L4 gives the quadratic iterate estimate g(g(n))\ge (g(n)-1)^2/(n-1) for n\ge 2. Substituting this into the original inequality via L5 yields the direct recurrence g(n+1)-g(n)\ge((g(n)-1)^2/(n-1))^r. But L6 states that such a recurrence has no positive-integer-valued solution when r>1/4, contradiction. Therefore no exponent larger than 1/4 is admissible. Finally, apply L7 to the set S using the facts 1/4\in S and (\forall r>1/4, r\notin S). This yields exactly that the largest real constant is 1/4, and it is attained by the explicit witness g(n)=n^2.

steps.derives: The exponent r=1/4 is admissible: there exists a function g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}, namely g(n)=n^2, such that g(n+1)-g(n)\ge (g(g(n)))^{1/4} for all n\in\mathbb{N}.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L1 with r=1/4. This gives a concrete witness function, so 1/4 belongs to the admissible set S.

steps.derives: Fix any real number r>1/4 and suppose, for contradiction, that there exists g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} with g(n+1)-g(n)\ge (g(g(n)))^r for all n. Then g is strictly increasing and satisfies g(n)\ge n for all n.
steps.trivial_justification: Since r>1/4 implies r\ge 0, L2 applies directly to the hypothetical witness g.

steps.derives: For the same hypothetical witness g from A2, the difference sequence d_n:=g(n+1)-g(n) is nondecreasing.
steps.trivial_justification: Because r>1/4>0, the positivity hypothesis needed for L3 holds, so L3 applies to the same g.

steps.derives:
For every integer n\ge 2, the hypothetical witness g satisfies
\[
g(g(n)) \ge \frac{(g(n)-1)^2}{n-1}.
\]
steps.trivial_justification: A3 gives that d_n is nondecreasing, and A2 gives that g is strictly increasing. Therefore all hypotheses of L4 are met, and the displayed bound follows for every n\ge 2.

steps.derives:
For every integer n\ge 2, the hypothetical witness g satisfies
\[
g(n+1)-g(n) \ge \left(\frac{(g(n)-1)^2}{n-1}\right)^r.
\]
steps.trivial_justification: L5 is exactly the consequence of combining the original inequality with the estimate obtained in A4.

steps.derives: The hypothesis from A5 is impossible when r>1/4. Therefore no function g can satisfy the original inequality for any exponent r>1/4.
steps.trivial_justification: A5 shows that any hypothetical witness for the original problem with r>1/4 would satisfy the direct one-step inequality excluded by L6. Hence the assumed witness cannot exist. Since the choice of r>1/4 was arbitrary, every exponent strictly larger than 1/4 is inadmissible.

steps.derives:
Let
\[
S = \{ r\in\mathbb{R} : \exists g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\text{ such that } g(n+1)-g(n)\ge (g(g(n)))^r \text{ for all } n\in\mathbb{N} \}.
\]
Then 1/4\in S by A1, and A6 shows that every r>1/4 is not in S. Therefore 1/4 is the largest real constant for which there exists such a function g; equivalently, \sup S=1/4, and the supremum is attained.
steps.trivial_justification: This is precisely the order-theoretic conclusion of L7 applied with the facts established in A1 and A6.
